title: The Ferryman

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha becomes Vasudeva's assistant. Vasudeva, a simple and attentive listener, teaches him to listen to the river, which shows that there is no such thing as time—the river is everywhere at once. Years pass peacefully. Gotama's monks pass by, carrying news that the Buddha is dying, and Kamala travels with her son to see him; she is bitten by a snake, recognizes Siddhartha at the ferry, and dies in his arms. Siddhartha keeps their son.

answerKey.answer: She died long ago; he has lived alone since
He pushes the oar harder to overcome the current
the place where one was born
Learning to listen from the flowing river
Vasudeva sees Kamala’s death as part of the same round as his wife’s.

People are drawn to the dying Buddha as if they had no choice. The evidence is “thus they flocked, like being drawn on by a magic spell, to where the great Buddha was awaiting his death” (The Ferryman, paragraph 43). “Flocked” and “magic spell” make the crowds sound like birds pulled by a force, which shows how much his life meant to them and sets up Kamala’s journey to him.

“And the curious people laughed and were discussing how foolishly and gullibly the common people were spreading such empty rumours.” (The Ferryman, paragraph 42). “Curious” shows that the visitors come for a spectacle, not to learn, and “gullibly” turns their scorn back on themselves: they mock others for believing what they cannot see. Together the words show that the ferrymen’s wisdom is invisible to people who come looking for magic.

Time moves from a slow loss to something overcome. In Sansara, “Years passed by; surrounded by the good life, Siddhartha hardly felt them fading away.” (Sansara, paragraph 2). In The Ferryman, “The years passed by, and nobody counted them.” (The Ferryman, paragraph 43). A competing reading finds the two passages alike, since in both he ignores the years. Yet in Sansara he fails to notice time while it ruins him, and at the river he lives beyond it, which is the river’s lesson.

The inverted sentence puts the length of the telling first: “Until late at night, lasted his tale.” (The Ferryman, paragraph 22). Ending on “his tale” makes his whole life a story told at last to a listener. A competing reading finds only a plain note of time. Yet the hours of telling show that Siddhartha needs to be heard, and Vasudeva’s patience prepares the next lesson of the chapter, the art of listening.

items.answerGuidance: In The Ferryman, paragraph 18, “recognise” after a long look makes the meeting slow and searching; the ferryman remembers the Samana in the rich man, which shows that he sees through appearances.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “The Ferryman”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Siddhartha becomes Vasudeva's assistant. Vasudeva, a simple and attentive listener, teaches him to listen to the river, which shows that there is no such thing as time—the river is everywhere at once. Years pass peacefully. Gotama's monks pass by, carrying news that the Buddha is dying, and Kamala…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The cause is Kamala’s arrival with their son (The Ferryman, paragraphs 45–53). Effect: her death leaves Siddhartha with a son, and love and worry come back into his life in the next chapter.

items.text: How does “The Ferryman” build on “By the River”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: in “By the River” he decided not to leave the river; here he acts on it, “By this river I want to stay, thought Siddhartha” (The Ferryman, paragraph 1).

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Vasudeva says he is no learned man and cannot teach (paragraph 29), yet his listening is the teaching; Kamala says she travels to the Buddha (paragraph 45), but her questions at death are about Siddhartha’s peace (paragraph 60).

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “What does the river teach that no person could?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should name listening and timelessness (The Ferryman, paragraphs 30 and 34) and add that the river teaches by example, not words, which Vasudeva says plainly: “The river has taught me to listen” (paragraph 27).

items.text: Where does theme appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with the river and time?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme of the river and time is stated in The Ferryman, paragraph 34 and applied to his life in paragraph 35: “I looked at my life, and it was also a river” (The Ferryman, paragraph 35).

items.text: Background: The image of the river echoes ancient ideas, such as Heraclitus's saying that one cannot step into the same river twice. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing Heraclitus’s saying shows Hesse’s twist: the river changes yet is everywhere at once (The Ferryman, paragraph 34), so for Siddhartha it teaches unity, not only change.

items.text: A critic might argue: “The listening river replaces human teachers; Kamala's peaceful death and the son's arrival begin a new test.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree in part: Siddhartha learns more from the river than from Vasudeva (paragraph 30). A text counterpoint: Vasudeva’s listening and example (paragraphs 23, 27) are still a human teacher’s work.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With patience as the standard, Vasudeva is wisest (paragraphs 23, 72); the boy, who whines and makes his tired mother stop to rest, is least wise, though he is a child (paragraphs 46–47).

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “The Ferryman” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about learning from the river?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Kamala’s view of her last hour (The Ferryman, paragraphs 57–64) works well: she sees peace in his eyes and wants it, which hides his own grief.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “The Ferryman”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘How is Kamala hurt?’ (snake, paragraph 47); why/how, ‘Why doesn’t Siddhartha feel sad?’ (paragraph 71); what if, ‘Should Siddhartha have gone to the Buddha too?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to love and attachment: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong: love returns as grief and as a son (The Ferryman, paragraphs 53, 65). Hesse now needs to show the cost of that love, which the next chapter does.

items.text: Is the symbolism in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective: the river’s lessons are given in dialogue and experience (paragraphs 32–40). Some readers find the timeless-river passages abstract.

items.text: Compare how “The Ferryman” treats learning from the river with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a story of a mentor who teaches by listening and quote “But more than Vasudeva could teach him, he was taught by the river.” (The Ferryman, paragraph 30)

items.text: Predict what “The Son” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: the boy is spoiled and used to having his way (“he was accustomed to having his way against her” (The Ferryman, paragraph 46)) and now lives with two old men. Prediction: conflict between Siddhartha and his son.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about learning from the river?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a burnt-out man who learns from a quiet mentor and nature, then meets a child he never knew. What must stay is the lesson of listening (paragraph 30).

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Why is Siddhartha not sad at Kamala’s death?’ The text answers: he has become “even richer and happier” by gaining a son and by seeing her peace (The Ferryman, paragraph 71).

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Kamala dies of a snakebite: “a small, black snake fled, by which Kamala had been bitten.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Ferryman, para. 47) The scene is peaceful and is followed by a funeral pyre.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Kamala is bitten by a snake and dies peacefully; the chapter also mentions drinking.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “How does Hesse make Kamala’s death feel peaceful rather than frightening?”

Analyze the river as the novel's central symbol, with Heracleitus as context. *(word)*
Argue how Kamala's peaceful death fits the river's teaching.
Integrate Plato's Cratylus on Heracleitus with your reading, with attribution.

Explain learning to listen from Vasudeva and the river, and Kamala’s peaceful death, using “this water ran and ran, incessantly it ran, and was nevertheless always there, was always at all times the same and yet new in every moment!” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Ferryman, para. 3), and compare one critical voice from this unit.

Apply a formal reading to learning to listen from Vasudeva and the river, and Kamala’s peaceful death: show how imagery and repetition in “this water ran and ran, incessantly it ran, and was nevertheless always there, was always at all times the same and yet new in every moment!” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Ferryman, para. 3) build its meaning.

Argue how learning to listen from Vasudeva and the river, and Kamala’s peaceful death advances the novel’s claim about teaching versus experience, testing “this water ran and ran, incessantly it ran, and was nevertheless always there, was always at all times the same and yet new in every moment!” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Ferryman, para. 3) against one later chapter.

Situate learning to listen from Vasudeva and the river, and Kamala’s peaceful death within scholarship on Hesse and European representations of Indian thought, stating method and contribution, with “this water ran and ran, incessantly it ran, and was nevertheless always there, was always at all times the same and yet new in every moment!” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Ferryman, para. 3) as anchor.
